response_text:
===FINDING 1===
LEAD: The 20-Gram-Panchayat sample records spending of Rs 51.96 crore less than planned across costed activities. The gap is broad-based across blocks and almost every asset category, rather than being confined to one block.
DETAIL: Across 5,630 costed activities planned from 2020-21 to 2025-26, 27 of 28 asset-category groupings showed the gap spread across the 16 sampled blocks. Rangeilunda had the largest recorded shortfall at Rs 9.11 crore, with Rs 2.73 crore spent against Rs 11.84 crore planned; Kalimela followed at Rs 5.90 crore, with Rs 1.76 crore spent against Rs 7.65 crore planned—about 23% utilisation in each. Banking Facilities was the sole exception, but the analysis found no clear pattern there. At the next review, ask blocks—starting with Rangeilunda and Kalimela—to reconcile planned costs, work status and recorded payments; these data show the gaps but not whether they reflect timing, incomplete work or record discrepancies.

===FINDING 1===
LEAD: Spending on costed activities in the 20-GP sample was Rs 51.96 crore below plan, and the gap is not confined to one block or asset category. Rangeilunda and Kalimela warrant particular review, with only about 23% of planned costs recorded as spent.
DETAIL: Across 5,630 costed activities, the underspending pattern appears across all 16 sampled blocks and 27 of 28 asset categories; Banking Facilities showed no clear pattern. Rangeilunda recorded Rs 2.73 crore spent against Rs 11.84 crore planned, while Kalimela recorded Rs 1.76 crore against Rs 7.65 crore. Review older incomplete activities, expenditure linkage and plan revisions across blocks rather than treating this as a single-block issue; the data does not show why the gaps arose.
===FINDING 5===
LEAD: For activities with sanction records, spending was Rs 5.02 crore below the sanctioned amount across the nine sampled districts. Ganjam had the largest recorded gap at Rs 1.68 crore and should be prioritised for reconciliation.
DETAIL: The shortfall appears across 27 of 28 asset categories rather than being confined to one district; Banking Facilities showed no clear pattern. Ganjam recorded Rs 4.61 crore spent against Rs 6.30 crore sanctioned, while Cuttack recorded the highest utilisation among the listed districts at 92.0%. Ask districts to reconcile unspent sanctions and activity status, but note that only about one in six activities has a sanction record, so these are not programme-wide utilisation rates.
===FINDING 7===
LEAD: Two unidentified output codes account for most planned untied funding for public works: Code 101 received Rs 34.88 crore and Code 105 Rs 16.90 crore. Their missing descriptions should be resolved before officials assess what this concentration represents.
DETAIL: Code 101 accounts for 62.1% and Code 105 for 30.1% of the Rs 56.20 crore planned untied funding in the sample, and both lead in 19 of the 20 GPs. Haldikudar follows a different pattern. Obtain or restore the definitions for these output codes and check Haldikudar’s coding and allocation mix; the present records cannot show what types of outputs these codes contain.
===FINDING 9===
LEAD: More than half of sampled public works—5,181 of 9,418 activities, or 55.0%—have no asset category recorded. This widespread classification gap limits meaningful review of what assets GPs are planning and creating.
DETAIL: “Uncategorised” is the largest group in 19 of the 20 GPs; Govindapur follows a different pattern. Buildings are the next-largest category but account for only 688 activities. Ask GPs to complete or correct asset-category fields, beginning with the 19 showing the common pattern, and review Govindapur’s practice as a possible reference point.
===FINDING 11===
LEAD: Activities still recorded as “Activity Approved” account for Rs 41.61 crore of the Rs 51.96 crore gap between planned cost and spending. Only Rs 14.00 lakh is recorded as spent against their Rs 41.75 crore planned cost.
DETAIL: This is the largest status-wise gap in 18 of the 20 GPs; Boipariguda and Laxmipur showed no clear pattern. Officials should age the approved activities, check whether work or payments have begun under another status, and reconcile the 13 rows incorrectly coded as “Buildings.” Completed works also show spending Rs 18,797 above plan, though on a small base, and may merit a record check; the data does not explain the discrepancies.
===FINDING 14===
LEAD: Nearly all General-category voucher spending on costed activities—Rs 28.59 crore, or 93.9%—is attached to works currently recorded as ongoing. Spending is also recorded against abandoned, approved and under-approval works, which merits status and voucher reconciliation.
DETAIL: Abandoned works carry Rs 1.15 crore of General-category spending, while approved and under-approval activities carry Rs 32.74 lakh and Rs 13.04 lakh respectively. The dominance of ongoing works appears in 18 of 20 GPs; Boipariguda and Laxmipur showed no clear pattern. Check whether statuses are current and whether vouchers are linked to the correct activity; these records alone do not establish that any payment was improper.
===FINDING 16===
LEAD: Of the expected beneficiaries recorded in the sample, 98.4%—2,03,534 people—are attached to activities still marked “Activity Approved.” Very few are linked to ongoing, abandoned or completed work.
DETAIL: The same pattern appears in 18 of the 20 GPs, while Boipariguda and Laxmipur showed no clear pattern. Beneficiary details exist for only 763 activities, and these figures are expected beneficiaries, not people actually served. Review whether activity statuses and beneficiary fields are being updated, particularly for completed works, before using these totals to assess delivery.
===FINDING 20===
LEAD: Half of planned untied funding for costed activities—Rs 30.07 crore, or 50.4%—is assigned to Theme 6, “Self-sufficient Infrastructure in Village.” Boipariguda and Kalimela depart from this common allocation pattern and should be discussed separately.
DETAIL: Theme 6 leads in 18 of the 20 GPs. In Boipariguda, “Unmapped theme” leads, indicating that the relevant focus areas have no theme mapping on file; across the sample, unmapped activities carry Rs 5.70 crore. In Kalimela, Theme 4, “Water Sufficient Village,” leads. Ask Boipariguda to correct or explain missing mappings and Kalimela to confirm that its theme allocation reflects its approved plan.
===FINDING 22===
LEAD: Code 101 accounts for Rs 2.49 crore of the Rs 2.54 crore gap between sanctioned and spent amounts for new works with sanction records. Officials should identify what this code represents before reviewing the outstanding sanctions.
DETAIL: Code 101 has the largest absolute gap in 19 of the 20 GPs and records Rs 14.94 crore spent against Rs 17.43 crore sanctioned, or 85.7%. Chikilli showed no clear pattern, while Code 110 records no spending against Rs 1.78 lakh sanctioned. Reconcile sanctions, payments and work status by code, noting that the code descriptions are missing and sanction-based figures cover only about one in six activities.
===FINDING 24===
LEAD: Every geotagged photo recorded for new works in this analysis—6,893 uploads—is linked to Code 101, although Code 101 represents only 32.8% of new-work activities. The absence of photos against all other output codes calls for an evidence-linkage and coding check.
DETAIL: Codes 102, 103, 109 and 110 show no photo uploads in this view, and the Code 101 concentration appears in 19 of the 20 GPs; Chikilli showed no clear pattern. Because none of the output codes has a description on file, the data cannot establish whether this reflects missing evidence, incorrect code mapping or a valid workflow distinction. Restore the code definitions and test whether photos are being linked to the correct activities.
===FINDING 25===
LEAD: Codes 101 and 105 have the largest gaps between planned cost and spending across every recorded beneficiary-purpose group. Code 101 is Rs 30.97 crore below plan and Code 105 is Rs 15.11 crore below plan.
DETAIL: Code 101 records Rs 15.88 crore spent against Rs 46.85 crore planned, or 33.9%, while Code 105 records Rs 7.32 crore against Rs 22.43 crore, or 32.6%. The pattern holds for activities serving the general public, General, SC and ST groups. As the code descriptions are missing, officials should first establish what the two codes represent, then review activity status, plan revisions and expenditure records; the data does not explain the gaps.
===FINDING 27===
LEAD: Planned tied funding is concentrated almost entirely in sanitation and drinking water: Rs 8.82 crore and Rs 8.42 crore respectively. This pattern holds across all four recorded beneficiary-purpose groups.
DETAIL: Sanitation accounts for 49.9% and drinking water for 47.7% of the Rs 17.66 crore in tied funding, while roads receive Rs 31.01 lakh and education Rs 8.05 lakh. Because tied grants are earmarked, this concentration is not by itself evidence of a problem. Officials should confirm that focus-area coding and approved plans align with the applicable funding conditions across General, SC, ST and general-public activities.
===FINDING 32===
LEAD: Chikilli has no sanctioned amount recorded in any of the six years from 2020-21 to 2025-26, despite accounting for 5.0% of activities in the sample. This is a clear record-reconciliation priority.
DETAIL: Chikilli is the lowest among the 20 GPs in every year, with Rs 0 recorded against the sample’s Rs 28.84 crore total sanctioned amount. This does not establish that no sanctions were issued, because sanction records exist for only about one in six activities. Check whether Chikilli’s sanctions are missing, unlinked or recorded elsewhere, and compare its submission practice with GPs that have complete sanction entries.
===FINDING 35===
LEAD: Spending recorded under grant components classified as “Other” remains the smallest category in every year, totalling Rs 1.02 crore or 3.6% of General-category voucher spending. Officials should verify that these components are correctly classified rather than assuming they are tied or untied grants.
DETAIL: Untied components account for Rs 16.75 crore and tied components for Rs 10.71 crore, compared with Rs 1.02 crore under “Other.” The same ranking holds from 2020-21 through 2025-26. Review the component codes behind “Other” and confirm whether this residual classification is valid; the figures alone do not indicate misclassification.
===FINDING 42===
LEAD: In every year, the smallest and largest GP population groups have the lowest total sanctioned amounts. GPs under 2,500 people received Rs 2.73 crore in recorded sanctions, while those with 10,000 people or more received Rs 4.82 crore.
DETAIL: The two middle population groups account for Rs 10.83 crore and Rs 10.47 crore respectively, but they also contain most of the sampled activity volume. These totals cover only the 20-GP sample and activities with sanction records, about one in six; they are not per-capita figures and do not establish unequal allocation. Before drawing conclusions, compare the number of GPs and activities in each size group, sanction-record completeness and per-capita amounts.

===FINDING 2===
LEAD: Planned-activity-linked spending in the 20-GP sample shows an overall upward trend, reaching Rs 5.92 crore in 2025-26, the highest annual total recorded.
DETAIL: The upward pattern appears whether the records are viewed monthly, quarterly or by fiscal year, although it was not a steady year-on-year rise: annual spending fell to Rs 3.66 crore in 2023-24 before increasing to Rs 5.06 crore in 2024-25 and Rs 5.92 crore in 2025-26. Reviews should examine the 2023-24 dip and confirm that the subsequent increase is supported by corresponding plans, sanctions, works and evidence; the data does not explain why the pattern occurred.

===FINDING 6===
LEAD: GPs in the smallest and largest population bands consistently recorded the lowest total cashbook payments in every year of the sample. This should not be read as lower spending intensity without accounting for how few records these groups contribute.
DETAIL: Across six years, GPs with 10,000 or more people recorded Rs 11.62 crore and those below 2,500 recorded Rs 6.62 crore, compared with Rs 27.77 crore for the 5,000–10,000 group and Rs 22.57 crore for the 2,500–5,000 group. However, the largest GPs had the highest average monthly payment per GP at Rs 8.07 lakh; officials should therefore compare GP-level monthly amounts and the number of GPs represented before questioning the lower totals.

===FINDING 8===
LEAD: GPs with populations between 2,500 and 10,000 accounted for three-quarters of all planned-activity-linked spending in the sample, and led in every fiscal year.
DETAIL: The 5,000–10,000 group recorded Rs 9.93 crore, or 41.4% of the total, while the 2,500–5,000 group recorded Rs 8.19 crore, or 34.1%. These groups also account for most vouchers in the sample, so the totals do not by themselves indicate better performance; reviews should compare spending per GP and verify whether activity links, works and supporting records are complete across all size bands.

===FINDING 10===
LEAD: Planned-activity-linked spending increased over the monthly series in every GP size band, with the largest sample-wide peaks occurring near the end of recent financial years.
DETAIL: March 2025 recorded Rs 1.05 crore, March 2026 Rs 99.60 lakh and March 2023 Rs 86.39 lakh, while April and December 2020 recorded no such spending. Officials should check whether the March concentrations are matched by timely sanctions, work progress and photo evidence, while recognising that the records show timing but do not establish the reason for it.

===FINDING 12===
LEAD: Receipt-voucher recording follows a recurring cycle across Mixed, SC-majority and ST-majority GPs, with several of the highest totals appearing in January–March quarters.
DETAIL: The engine detected a repeating 12-quarter pattern in all three social-composition groups. Across the sample, 2024-Q1 had 395 receipt vouchers, while 2023-Q2 had only 43; officials should review whether these recurring peaks and troughs reflect expected fund-release and recording schedules or delayed entry, without assuming a cause from the pattern alone.

===FINDING 15===
LEAD: Mixed-composition GPs accounted for Rs 19.04 crore, or 79.4%, of all planned-activity-linked spending in the sample and held the majority in every fiscal year.
DETAIL: SC-majority GPs accounted for Rs 2.54 crore and ST-majority GPs for Rs 2.41 crore. Mixed GPs also account for 82.7% of the vouchers represented, so their spending share largely reflects the sample’s record distribution; officials should compare GP-level spending and documentation rather than treating these totals as evidence of unequal performance or allocation.

===FINDING 18===
LEAD: SC-majority GPs had the lowest average monthly cashbook payments in five of the six years reviewed; 2025-26 did not follow this pattern.
DETAIL: Across the full period, the average monthly payment per GP was Rs 2.31 lakh for SC-majority GPs, compared with Rs 4.38 lakh for ST-majority and Rs 5.30 lakh for Mixed GPs. The next review should identify what changed in the 2025-26 ranking and examine GP-level payment and work records; these averages show a difference but do not establish its cause or whether needs and allocations were comparable.

===FINDING 21===
LEAD: Bhubaneswar recorded the highest number of payment vouchers among the 16 sampled blocks in five of six years, accounting for 2,135 vouchers, or 25.0% of the total.
DETAIL: The pattern was not clear in 2024-25. The next-highest totals were Rangeilunda with 945 vouchers and Bheden with 885, while Balisankara and Lahunipara recorded 178 and 181 respectively; officials should check whether the wide variation reflects the number and size of sampled GPs, genuine transaction volumes, or differences in voucher recording and consolidation.

===FINDING 26===
LEAD: Monthly sanction counts changed markedly around October 2020 in three of the four GP size bands; GPs with 10,000 or more people showed their main shift later, around January 2021.
DETAIL: The shift was detected for GPs below 2,500, between 2,500 and 5,000, and between 5,000 and 10,000 people, but the analysis does not state that the change was necessarily an increase or explain it. Officials should reconcile sanction dates and any recording or process changes around October 2020 and January 2021, particularly because the timing differs for the largest GPs.

===FINDING 28===
LEAD: Average monthly cashbook payments show a repeating annual cycle in three GP size bands, but GPs with 10,000 or more people follow a different pattern.
DETAIL: March was among the highest months in several years, including Rs 22.47 lakh per GP in March 2022 and Rs 20.12 lakh in March 2026. Officials should test whether March payment concentrations align with completed works and supporting evidence, and separately review the largest GPs rather than applying the same seasonal expectation to them; the data does not establish why the cycles differ.

===FINDING 34===
LEAD: Payment-voucher volumes show recurring cycles when viewed by month and quarter, but there is no clear recurring pattern across fiscal years.
DETAIL: Annual totals varied from 1,003 vouchers in 2023-24 to 1,985 in 2025-26. Officials should focus reconciliation on recurring within-year peaks and troughs and ask whether voucher entry is timely, while treating year-to-year changes separately because the analysis found no clear fiscal-year cycle.

===FINDING 36===
LEAD: Among Mixed-composition GPs, the smallest and largest population bands had the lowest totals on seven of nine financial and activity measures. This appears closely related to their small representation in the sample and should not be treated as evidence of lower activity per GP.
DETAIL: The pattern covers total payments, receipts, payment and receipt vouchers, planned-activity-linked spending, sanctions and sanctioned amounts; it does not hold clearly for average monthly payment or receipt amounts. The largest GPs actually averaged Rs 8.80 lakh in monthly payments per GP and the smallest Rs 6.08 lakh, above both middle-size groups, so officials should use per-GP comparisons before flagging low totals.

===FINDING 37===
LEAD: Among Mixed-composition GPs, the two middle population bands led on seven of nine total financial and activity measures, but not clearly on average monthly inflows or outflows per GP.
DETAIL: GPs between 2,500 and 10,000 people account for most of the records in scope: 48.7% of vouchers are from the 5,000–10,000 band and 37.7% from the 2,500–5,000 band. Their leading totals therefore do not establish higher activity intensity; reviews should compare individual GPs and monthly averages, including the higher Rs 8.80 lakh average monthly payment recorded for the largest GPs.

===FINDING 44===
LEAD: Sanction counts increased over the six-year period for Mixed and SC-majority GPs, while ST-majority GPs showed no clear trend.
DETAIL: Across the full sample, annual sanctions reached 404 in 2024-25 and 485 in 2025-26, the highest total recorded. Officials should separately review the year-by-year sanction pipeline for ST-majority GPs and reconcile it with proposed activities and sanctioned amounts; the differing pattern does not by itself show delay, shortfall or any underlying cause.

===FINDING 4===
LEAD: Recorded expenditure was below plan across all highlighted blocks, with the average gap ranging from Rs 87.50 lakh per GP in Bhubaneswar to Rs 5.90 crore in Kalimela. The largest gaps warrant reconciliation of planned costs against expenditure records.
DETAIL: For Mixed and SC-majority GPs, the gap is broadly spread across blocks; no clear distribution was found for ST-majority GPs. Bheden averaged Rs 5.60 crore below plan per GP and Kalimela Rs 5.90 crore, compared with Rs 87.50 lakh in Bhubaneswar and Rs 90.62 lakh in Lahunipara. Most cited block averages are based on one GP, while Bhubaneswar covers three, so these figures should be checked GP by GP and not treated as block-wide performance.

===FINDING 13===
LEAD: The recorded gap between sanctions and expenditure varies sharply across the 20 sampled GPs—from no gap in Chikilli to Rs 85.77 lakh below sanction in Sharagada. Sharagada and Dutimendi should be prioritised for reconciliation.
DETAIL: Sharagada recorded expenditure Rs 85.77 lakh below sanction and Dutimendi Rs 57.38 lakh below, while Chikilli recorded no gap; Govindapur, Hirlipali, Barimunda and Bhatigaon were between Rs 6.94 lakh and Rs 10.81 lakh below sanction. The gaps are broadly spread among Mixed and SC-majority GPs, but no clear pattern was found among ST-majority GPs. Review whether the larger differences reflect incomplete works, pending payments or records awaiting update; the data does not establish which explanation applies.

===FINDING 19===
LEAD: Mixed-composition GPs lead on 57 of 74 measures, but this largely reflects their much larger presence in the sample rather than evidence of better performance. Reviews should focus on the exceptions and on per-GP figures, not group totals alone.
DETAIL: Mixed GPs account for 76.0% of the 12,704 activities, compared with 12.7% for SC-majority and 11.3% for ST-majority GPs. Exceptions include completed works and average tap-water coverage, where ST-majority GPs lead, and the average plan–expenditure difference, where SC-majority GPs lead; several financial and approval averages show no clear pattern. Photo evidence also differs: 488.5 uploads per ST-majority GP, 441.1 per Mixed GP and 224.3 per SC-majority GP, but these averages represent only two, 15 and three GPs respectively. Ask for GP-level comparisons before drawing conclusions by social composition.

===FINDING 23===
LEAD: Across the nine sampled districts, recorded expenditure was Rs 51.96 crore below plan. Ganjam and Bargarh account for the largest district-level gaps and should be first in line for reconciliation.
DETAIL: Ganjam recorded a gap of Rs 17.85 crore and Bargarh Rs 9.72 crore, compared with Rs 1.24 crore in Rayagada and Rs 2.63 crore in Khordha. Their larger totals partly coincide with higher activity volumes—21.4% of activities in Ganjam and 24.1% in Bargarh—so totals should be read alongside per-GP figures; Bargarh averaged Rs 2.43 crore below plan per GP, while Khordha averaged Rs 87.50 lakh. The gap is broadly spread across districts for Mixed and SC-majority GPs, with no clear pattern for ST-majority GPs; the records do not show why the differences arose.

LEAD: The 2,500–5,000 and 5,000–10,000 population groups lead 48 of 74 measures, but this is mainly a pattern in totals and should not be read as stronger GP performance. These groups account for 37.8% and 43.8% respectively of the 8,108 activities examined.

Officials should compare totals with per-GP figures before drawing conclusions and treat the smallest and largest groups cautiously, as each average is based on only one GP.
